text: Moore woke him and told him the Germans had sent men forward to take the American surrender. According to Moore's account to the Army historian S. L. A. Marshall, McAuliffe's first answer was a single word. Nuts. In the operations room, he read the type sheets. By Canard's account, he asked whether the Germans wanted to surrender. Canard told him, No, sir, they want us to surrender. McAuliffe said, us surrender? Ah, nuts. And crumpled the paper. He then left to visit a unit on the west side of the perimeter that had beaten off a German probe. According to the staff accounts, nobody in the room argued for giving up. The only open matter was what to say, and the two hours were running down. When McAuliffe came back, Moore reminded him that the four Germans were still waiting at the company F outpost and that Custom called for a written reply. McAuliffe sat down with a pencil and paper and said he did not know what to tell them. Canard answered that what the general had said at first would be hard to beat. McAuliffe asked what he meant. Canard said, Sir, you said nuts. The staff officers in the room laughed and agreed. McAuliffe dictated the reply, and the sergeant typed it centered on a single sheet. To the German commander, N-U-T-S. The American commander. That was all of it. Colonel Joseph Harper of the 327th Glider Infantry took the sheet to the outpost. McAuliffe told him to hand it over and not to go into the German lines. Hanke read it and asked whether the reply was negative or affirmative, and if it was affirmative, he would negotiate further. Harper told him it was decidedly not affirmative, and that if the Germans kept attacking, their losses would be tremendous. Private First Class Ernest Premitz put the meaning into German as a suggestion to go to the devil. Hanke's last words in Harper's account were that the Germans would kill many Americans and that this was war. He and Wagner saluted and walked back toward their lines. The word did not change the plan. The decision it announced was the one the staff had already made to stay inside the circle and hold it with 10 rounds of gun and a relief column of unknown arrival. The artillery bombardment the note promised did not come. On December 23, the cold front cleared the sky and 241 C-47 transports dropped 144 tons of ammunition, medical supplies and rations into the perimeter, while P-47 fighters struck German armor around the town. That night, December 24, German bombers raided Bastogne, a direct hit on the aid station of Combat Command B killed a Belgian nurse, René Le Maire, and about 30 wounded American soldiers. Makalov's Christmas message given to every man in the pocket told them the story of the surrender demand and the reply. On Christmas morning, the German 15th Panzer Grenadier Division and the 26th Volksgrenadier Division attacked the Western perimeter. 18 German tanks broke through the line and the 502nd Parachute Infantry, the 327th Glider Infantry and the 705th Tank Destroyer Battalion destroyed all of them. At 10 minutes to five on the afternoon of December 26, the lead tank of Task Force Abrams, a Sherman named Cobra King from the 4th Armored Division, reached the engineers of Company C, 326th Airborne Engineer Battalion at the southern edge of the pocket. The road was open. The 101st did not leave. It went on fighting around Bastogne into January. Makalov held that paper because he was the senior officer in camp when the two generals above him were in Washington and England. The word came from his own reaction and a staff officer saw that it could serve as the reply. It committed him to the plan the room had already chosen, a defense in place. And the clearing weather and the 4th Armored Division made that plan survivable. Maxwell Taylor rejoined the division that night and took command back.
